label: Definition 7.3.3 .

label: Definition 13.2.1 . Linear Ordering.
definition: Linear Ordering.
long_description: Linear Ordering. A number field is said to be linearly ordered if there is a relation, denoted “ \(\lt \) ”, on the elements of the field which satisfies all of the following for all \(x, y\text{,}\) and \(z\) in the field. For all numbers \(x\) and \(y\) in the field, exactly one of the following holds: \(\displaystyle x\lt y\) \(\displaystyle x=y\) \(\displaystyle y\lt x\) If \(x\lt y\text{,}\) then \(x+z\lt y+z\) for all \(z\) in the field. If \(x\lt y\text{,}\) and \(0\lt z\text{,}\) then \(x\cdot z \lt y\cdot z\text{.}\) If \(x\lt y\) and \(y\lt z\) then \(x\lt z\text{.}\) in-context

label: Theorem 12.0.10 .

Then if the trigonometric series \(\sum_{n=0}^\infty\left(c_n\cos n\pi x\,+d_n\sin n\pi x\right)\) is zero for all \(x\in\RR-S\text{,}\) then all of the coefficients of the series vanish. in-context

label: Definition 11.1.3 .
definition: Let \(S\) be a subset of the real number system and let \(\left(f_n\right)=\left(f_1,f_2,f_3,\,\ldots\right)\) be a sequence of functions defined on \(S\text{.}\) Let \(f\) be a function defined on \(S\) as well.

We say that \(\left(f_n\right)\) converges to \(f\) uniformly on \(S\) provided \(\forall\ \eps>0,\,\exists\ N\) such that \(n>N\Rightarrow|f_n(x)-f(x)|\lt \eps\text{ , } \forall\ x\in S\text{.}\) In this case we write \(f_n\unif f\) on \(S\text{.}\) in-context

label: Theorem 9.2.12 .
definition: Suppose \(f\) is continuous at \(a\) and \(g\) is continuous at \(f(a)\text{.}\) Then \(g\circ f\) is continuous at \(a.\) (Note that \((g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x))\text{.}\) ) in-context.

label: Theorem 11.2.30 .
definition: Suppose \(\sum a_n\) converges absolutely and let \(s=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n\text{.}\) Then any rearrangement of \(\sum a_n\) must converge to \(s\text{.}\) in-context.

label: Theorem 12.0.3 .
definition: Cantor, (1871) If the trigonometric series \begin{equation*} \sum_{n=0}^\infty\left(c_n\cos n\pi x\,+d_n\sin n\pi x\right) = 0\text{,} \end{equation*} for all but finitely many \(x\in\RR\) then all of its coefficients vanish.

label: Theorem 11.2.20 . Cauchy Criterion.
definition: Cauchy Criterion.
long_description: Cauchy Criterion. The series \(\sum_{k=0}^\infty a_k\) converges if and only if \(\forall \eps>0\text{,}\) \(\exists N\) such that if \(m>n>N\) then \(|\sum_{k=n+1}^ma_k|\lt \eps\text{.}\) in-context

label: Theorem 11.2.15 .

label: Definition 13.2.22 .
definition: Addition Let \(\alpha, \beta\in\RR\text{.}\) Then \begin{equation*} \alpha+\beta= \begin{cases}-(\abs{\alpha}+\abs{\beta}) \amp \text{ if \(\alpha\lt 0, \beta\lt 0 \) } \\ \ \ \ \abs{\alpha}-\abs{\beta}\amp \text{ if \(\alpha>0, \beta\lt 0, \abs{\alpha}>\abs{\beta} \)} \\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \,0 \amp \text{ if \(\alpha>0, \beta\lt 0, \abs{\alpha}=\abs{\beta} \)} \\ -(\abs{\alpha}-\abs{\beta}) \amp \text{ if \(\alpha>0, \beta\lt 0, \abs{\alpha}\lt \abs{\beta} \)} \\ \ \ \ \ \ \beta+\alpha \amp \text{ if \(\alpha\lt 0, \beta>0 \) } \\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \,\beta{} \amp \text{ if \(\alpha=0 \) } \\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \,\alpha \amp \text{ if \(\beta=0 \) } \end{cases} \text{.} \end{equation*} in-context.
long_description: Addition Let \(\alpha, \beta\in\RR\text{.}\) Then \begin{equation*} \alpha+\beta= \begin{cases}-(\abs{\alpha}+\abs{\beta}) \amp \text{ if \(\alpha\lt 0, \beta\lt 0 \) } \\ \ \ \ \abs{\alpha}-\abs{\beta}\amp \text{ if \(\alpha>0, \beta\lt 0, \abs{\alpha}>\abs{\beta} \)} \\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \,0 \amp \text{ if \(\alpha>0, \beta\lt 0, \abs{\alpha}=\abs{\beta} \)} \\ -(\abs{\alpha}-\abs{\beta}) \amp \text{ if \(\alpha>0, \beta\lt 0, \abs{\alpha}\lt \abs{\beta} \)} \\ \ \ \ \ \ \beta+\alpha \amp \text{ if \(\alpha\lt 0, \beta>0 \) } \\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \,\beta{} \amp \text{ if \(\alpha=0 \) } \\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \,\alpha \amp \text{ if \(\beta=0 \) } \end{cases} \text{.} \end{equation*} in-context

label: Theorem 7.2.15 .
definition: Squeeze Theorem for Sequences Let \(\left(r_n\right),\left(s_n\right)\text{,}\) and \(\left(t_n\right)\) be sequences of real numbers with \(r_n\leq s_n\leq t_n,\forall\) positive integers \(n\text{.}\) Suppose \(\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}r_n=s=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}t_n\text{.}\) Then \(\left(s_n\right)\) must converge and \(\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}s_n=s\text{.}\) in-context.
long_description: Squeeze Theorem for Sequences Let \(\left(r_n\right),\left(s_n\right)\text{,}\) and \(\left(t_n\right)\) be sequences of real numbers with \(r_n\leq s_n\leq t_n,\forall\) positive integers \(n\text{.}\) Suppose \(\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}r_n=s=\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}t_n\text{.}\) Then \(\left(s_n\right)\) must converge and \(\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}s_n=s\text{.}\) in-context

label: Theorem 13.2.14 .
definition: Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be cuts.

label: Theorem 5.1.9 .
definition: If \(f^\prime,\,f^{\prime\prime},\,\ldots,\,f^{(n+1)}\) are all continuous on an interval containing \(a\) and \(x\text{,}\) then \begin{align*} f(x)=f(a)+\frac{f^{\prime}(a)}{1!}(x-a)+\frac{f^{\prime \prime}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^2\amp +\cdots+\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(x-a)^n\\ \amp + \frac{1}{n!}\int_{t=a}^xf^{(n+1)}(t)(x-t)^n\dx{t}\text{.} \end{align*} in-context.
long_description: If \(f^\prime,\,f^{\prime\prime},\,\ldots,\,f^{(n+1)}\) are all continuous on an interval containing \(a\) and \(x\text{,}\) then \begin{align*} f(x)=f(a)+\frac{f^{\prime}(a)}{1!}(x-a)+\frac{f^{\prime \prime}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^2\amp +\cdots+\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(x-a)^n\\ \amp + \frac{1}{n!}\int_{t=a}^xf^{(n+1)}(t)(x-t)^n\dx{t}\text{.} \end{align*} in-context

definition: Suppose every Cauchy sequence converges.

definition: A continuous function defined on a closed, bounded interval must be bounded.
long_description: A continuous function defined on a closed, bounded interval must be bounded. That is, let \(f\) be a continuous function defined on \([\,a,b]\text{.}\) Then there exists a positive real number \(B\) such that \(|f(x)|\leq B\) for all \(x\in[\,a,b]\text{.}\) in-context

label: Definition 13.2.13 .
definition: Let \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) be cuts.

label: Definition 13.2.12 .
definition: Dedekind Cut A set of positive rational numbers is called a cut if Take special notice that we are not using the negative rational numbers or zero to build our cuts.
long_description: Dedekind Cut A set of positive rational numbers is called a cut if Take special notice that we are not using the negative rational numbers or zero to build our cuts. The reason for this will become clear shortly. Property I It contains a positive rational number but does not contain all positive rational numbers. Property II Every positive rational number in the set is less than every positive rational number not in the set. Property III There is no element of the set which is greater than every other element of the set. in-context

label: Definition 13.2.4 .
definition: Let \(x=\left(s_n\right)_{n=1}^\infty\) and \(y=\left(\sigma_n\right)_{n=1}^\infty\) be Cauchy sequences in \(\QQ\text{.}\) \(x\) and \(y\) are said to be equivalent if they satisfy the following property: For every \(\eps>0\text{,}\) \(\eps\in\QQ\text{,}\) there is a rational number \(N\) such that for all \(n>N\text{,}\) \(n\in\NN\text{,}\) \begin{equation*} \abs{s_n-\sigma_n}\lt \eps\text{.} \end{equation*} We will denote equivalence by writing, \(x\equiv y\text{.}\) in-context.
long_description: Let \(x=\left(s_n\right)_{n=1}^\infty\) and \(y=\left(\sigma_n\right)_{n=1}^\infty\) be Cauchy sequences in \(\QQ\text{.}\) \(x\) and \(y\) are said to be equivalent if they satisfy the following property: For every \(\eps>0\text{,}\) \(\eps\in\QQ\text{,}\) there is a rational number \(N\) such that for all \(n>N\text{,}\) \(n\in\NN\text{,}\) \begin{equation*} \abs{s_n-\sigma_n}\lt \eps\text{.} \end{equation*} We will denote equivalence by writing, \(x\equiv y\text{.}\) in-context

label: Theorem 9.4.8 .
definition: Rolle's Theorem Suppose \(f^\prime\) exists for every \(x\in(a,b)\text{,}\) \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\text{,}\) and \begin{equation*} f(a)=f(b) \text{.} \end{equation*} Then there is a real number \(c\in(a,b)\) such that \begin{equation*} f^\prime(c)=0 \text{.} \end{equation*} in-context.
long_description: Rolle's Theorem Suppose \(f^\prime\) exists for every \(x\in(a,b)\text{,}\) \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\text{,}\) and \begin{equation*} f(a)=f(b) \text{.} \end{equation*} Then there is a real number \(c\in(a,b)\) such that \begin{equation*} f^\prime(c)=0 \text{.} \end{equation*} in-context

label: Definition 4.2.1 .
definition: A power series centered at \(\boldsymbol{a}\) is a series of the form \begin{equation*} \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(x-a)^n=a_0+a_1(x-a)+a_2(x-a)^2+\cdots\text{.} \end{equation*} Often we will focus on the behavior of power series \(\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n\text{,}\) centered around \(0\text{,}\) as the series centered around other values of \(a\) are obtained by shifting a series centered at \(0\text{.}\) in-context.
long_description: A power series centered at \(\boldsymbol{a}\) is a series of the form \begin{equation*} \sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(x-a)^n=a_0+a_1(x-a)+a_2(x-a)^2+\cdots\text{.} \end{equation*} Often we will focus on the behavior of power series \(\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nx^n\text{,}\) centered around \(0\text{,}\) as the series centered around other values of \(a\) are obtained by shifting a series centered at \(0\text{.}\) in-context

label: Theorem 5.2.2 .
definition: Let \(a\) be any real number.

label: Theorem 10.1.4 .
definition: Suppose that we have two sequences \(\left(x_n\right)\) and \(\left(y_n\right)\) satisfying all of the assumptions of the Nested Interval Property.
long_description: Suppose that we have two sequences \(\left(x_n\right)\) and \(\left(y_n\right)\) satisfying all of the assumptions of the Nested Interval Property. If \(c\) is the unique number such that \(x_n\leq c\leq y_n\) for all \(n\text{,}\) then \(\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}x_n=c\) and \(\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}y_n=c\text{.}\) in-context

label: Definition 12.1.4 .
definition: Any set which can be put into one-to-one correspondence with \(\NN=\left\{1,2,3,\ldots\right\}\) is called a countably infinite set.
long_description: Any set which can be put into one-to-one correspondence with \(\NN=\left\{1,2,3,\ldots\right\}\) is called a countably infinite set. Any set which is either finite or countably infinite is said to be countable . in-context

label: Definition 13.2.21 .
definition: Multiplication Let \(\alpha, \beta\in\RR\text{.}\) Then \begin{equation*} \alpha\cdot\beta = \begin{cases}-\abs{\alpha}\abs{\beta}\amp \text{ if \(\alpha>0,\beta\lt 0\) or \(\alpha\lt 0, \beta>0,\) } \\ \ \ \,\abs{\alpha}\abs{\beta}\amp \text{ if \(\alpha\lt 0,\beta\lt 0,\) } \\ \ \ \ \ \ \, 0\amp \text{ if \(\alpha=0\) or \(\beta=0.\) } {} \end{cases} \end{equation*} in-context.
long_description: Multiplication Let \(\alpha, \beta\in\RR\text{.}\) Then \begin{equation*} \alpha\cdot\beta = \begin{cases}-\abs{\alpha}\abs{\beta}\amp \text{ if \(\alpha>0,\beta\lt 0\) or \(\alpha\lt 0, \beta>0,\) } \\ \ \ \,\abs{\alpha}\abs{\beta}\amp \text{ if \(\alpha\lt 0,\beta\lt 0,\) } \\ \ \ \ \ \ \, 0\amp \text{ if \(\alpha=0\) or \(\beta=0.\) } {} \end{cases} \end{equation*} in-context

label: Definition 7.1.1 .

long_description: Let \(\left(s_n\right)=\left(s_1,s_2,s_3,\ldots\right)\) be a sequence of real numbers. We say that \(\left(\boldsymbol{s}_{\boldsymbol{n}}\right)\) converges to 0 and write \(\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}s_n=0\) provided for any \(\eps>0\text{,}\) there is a real number \(N\) such that if \(n>N\text{,}\) then \(|s_n|\lt \eps\text{.}\) in-context

label: Theorem 10.1.6 .
definition: Suppose \(a\in\mathbb{R},\,a\geq 0\text{.}\) There exists a real number \(c\geq 0\) such that \(c^2=a\text{.}\) in-context.

long_description: Suppose \(a, b, c, d \in\NN\) be integers. There is a number \(\alpha\in\QQ\) such that \(M\alpha=a/b\) and \(N\alpha=c/d\) where \(M\) and \(N\) are also integers. in-context

label: Definition 10.4.2 . Least Upper Bound Property ( LUBP ).
definition: Least Upper Bound Property ( LUBP ).
long_description: Least Upper Bound Property ( LUBP ). Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) and let \(b\) be a real number. We say that \(b\) is the least upper bound of \(S\) provided \(b\geq x\) for all \(x\in S\text{.}\) ( \(b\) is an upper bound of \(S\) ) If \(c\geq x\) for all \(x\in S\text{,}\) then \(c\geq b\text{.}\) (Any upper bound of \(S\) is at least as big as \(b\text{.}\) ) In this case, we also say that \(b\) is the supremum of \(S\) and we write \begin{equation*} b=\sup\left(S\right)\text{.} \end{equation*} in-context

label: Theorem 10.2.1 .
definition: Intermediate Value Theorem Suppose \(f(x)\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and \(v\) is any real number between \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\text{.}\) Then there exists a real number \(c\in[\,a,b]\) such that \(f(c)=v\text{.}\) in-context.
long_description: Intermediate Value Theorem Suppose \(f(x)\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and \(v\) is any real number between \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\text{.}\) Then there exists a real number \(c\in[\,a,b]\) such that \(f(c)=v\text{.}\) in-context

label: Definition 11.1.2 .
definition: Let \(S\) be a subset of the real number system and let \(\left(f_n\right)=\left(f_1,f_2,f_3,\,\ldots\right)\) be a sequence of functions defined on \(S\text{.}\) Let \(f\) be a function defined on \(S\) as well.
long_description: Let \(S\) be a subset of the real number system and let \(\left(f_n\right)=\left(f_1,f_2,f_3,\,\ldots\right)\) be a sequence of functions defined on \(S\text{.}\) Let \(f\) be a function defined on \(S\) as well. We say that \(\left(f_n\right)\) converges to \(f\) pointwise on \(S\) provided that for all \(x\in S\text{,}\) the sequence of real numbers \(\left(f_n(x)\right)\) converges to the number \(f(x)\text{.}\) In this case we write \(\,f_n\ptwise f\) on \(S\text{.}\) in-context

label: Theorem 11.2.11 .
definition: Suppose \(\left(s_n\right)\) is a sequence of real numbers which converges to \(s\text{.}\) Then \(\left(s_n\right)\) is a Cauchy sequence.
long_description: Suppose \(\left(s_n\right)\) is a sequence of real numbers which converges to \(s\text{.}\) Then \(\left(s_n\right)\) is a Cauchy sequence. in-context

label: Theorem 5.1.1 .
definition: If \(f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(x-a)^n\text{,}\) then \(a_n=\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}\text{,}\) where \(f^{(n)}(a)\) represents the \(n^{th}\) derivative of \(f\) evaluated at \(a\text{.}\) in-context.
long_description: If \(f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n(x-a)^n\text{,}\) then \(a_n=\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}\text{,}\) where \(f^{(n)}(a)\) represents the \(n^{th}\) derivative of \(f\) evaluated at \(a\text{.}\) in-context

label: Definition 13.2.7 .
definition: If \begin{equation*} x= \left\{\left.\left(s_n\right)_{k=1}^\infty \right| \left(s_n\right)_{k=1}^\infty \text{ is Cauchy in \(\QQ\) } \right\} \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} y= \left\{\left.\left(\sigma_n\right)_{k=1}^\infty \right| \left(\sigma_n\right)_{k=1}^\infty \text{ is Cauchy in \(\QQ\) } \right\} \end{equation*} then we define the following: Addition:.
long_description: If \begin{equation*} x= \left\{\left.\left(s_n\right)_{k=1}^\infty \right| \left(s_n\right)_{k=1}^\infty \text{ is Cauchy in \(\QQ\) } \right\} \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} y= \left\{\left.\left(\sigma_n\right)_{k=1}^\infty \right| \left(\sigma_n\right)_{k=1}^\infty \text{ is Cauchy in \(\QQ\) } \right\} \end{equation*} then we define the following: Addition:. \(\displaystyle x+y = \left\{\left.\left(t_n\right)_{k=1}^\infty \right| t_k = s_k+\sigma_k, \forall (s_n) \in x, \text{ and } (\sigma_n)\in y\right\}\) Multiplication:. \(\displaystyle x\cdot y = \left\{\left.\left(t_n\right)_{k=1}^\infty \right| t_k = s_k\sigma_k, \forall (s_n) \in x, \text{ and } (\sigma_n)\in y\right\}\) in-context

label: Theorem 7.2.4 .
definition: If \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}a_n=a\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}b_n=b\text{,}\) then \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left(a_n+b_n\right)=a+b\text{.}\) in-context.
long_description: If \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}a_n=a\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}b_n=b\text{,}\) then \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left(a_n+b_n\right)=a+b\text{.}\) in-context

label: Definition 11.2.10 .
definition: Let \(\left(s_n\right)\) be a sequence of real numbers.
long_description: Let \(\left(s_n\right)\) be a sequence of real numbers. We say that \(\left(s_n\right)\) is a Cauchy sequence if for any \(\eps>0\text{,}\) there exists a real number \(N\) such that if \(m,n>N\text{,}\) then \(|s_m-s_n|\lt \eps\text{.}\) in-context

label: Definition 7.1.11 .
definition: Let \(\left(s_n\right)=\left(s_1,s_2,s_3,\ldots\right)\) be a sequence of real numbers and let \(s\) be a real number.
long_description: Let \(\left(s_n\right)=\left(s_1,s_2,s_3,\ldots\right)\) be a sequence of real numbers and let \(s\) be a real number. We say that \(\left(\boldsymbol{s}_{\boldsymbol{n}}\right)\) {converges to} \(\boldsymbol{s}\) and write \(\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}s_n=s\) provided for any \(\eps>0\text{,}\) there is a real number \(N\) such that if \(n>N\text{,}\) then \(|s_n-s|\lt \eps\text{.}\) in-context

label: Definition 12.0.7 .
definition: Let \(S\subseteq\RR\text{.}\) The set of all limit points of \(S\) is called the derived set of \(S\text{.}\) The derived set is denoted \(S^{\prime}\text{.}\) in-context.

label: Theorem 12.1.3 .
definition: Cantor, (1874) Let \(S=\left(s_n\right)_{n=1}^\infty\) be a sequence of real numbers.
long_description: Cantor, (1874) Let \(S=\left(s_n\right)_{n=1}^\infty\) be a sequence of real numbers. There is a real number \(c\text{,}\) which is not in \(S\text{.}\) To streamline things, we are abusing notation here as we are letting \(S\) denote both the sequence (which is ordered) and the underlying (unordered) set of entries in the sequence. in-context

label: Theorem 7.2.12 .
definition: Suppose \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}a_n=a\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}b_n=b\text{.}\) Also suppose \(b\neq 0\) and \(b_n\neq 0,\forall\,n\text{.}\) Then \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left(\frac{a_n}{b_n}\right)=\frac{a}{b}\text{.}\) in-context.
long_description: Suppose \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}a_n=a\) and \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}b_n=b\text{.}\) Also suppose \(b\neq 0\) and \(b_n\neq 0,\forall\,n\text{.}\) Then \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left(\frac{a_n}{b_n}\right)=\frac{a}{b}\text{.}\) in-context

label: Theorem 8.1.1 .
definition: Taylor's series If there exists a real number \(B\) such that \(|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\leq B\) for all nonnegative integers \(n\) and for all \(t\) on an interval containing \(a\) and \(x\text{,}\) then \begin{equation*} \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left(\frac{1}{n!}\int_{t=a}^xf^{(n+1)}(t)(x-t)^n\dx{ t}\right)=0 \end{equation*} and so \begin{equation*} f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(x-a)^n.{} \end{equation*} in-context.
long_description: Taylor's series If there exists a real number \(B\) such that \(|f^{(n+1)}(t)|\leq B\) for all nonnegative integers \(n\) and for all \(t\) on an interval containing \(a\) and \(x\text{,}\) then \begin{equation*} \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\left(\frac{1}{n!}\int_{t=a}^xf^{(n+1)}(t)(x-t)^n\dx{ t}\right)=0 \end{equation*} and so \begin{equation*} f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(x-a)^n.{} \end{equation*} in-context

label: Definition 12.1.5 .
definition: If two sets can be put into one-to-one correspondence then they are said to have the same cardinality.
